From Us to You

Plant Care Advice

Plain language, no fuss. The stuff we actually tell customers when they buy a plant from us.

The Fundamentals

Most plants die from one of four things.

Get these right and you'll keep most plants alive indefinitely. We promise they're simpler than the internet makes them look.

Watering

Most people overwater. The most reliable test: stick your finger an inch into the soil. If it's damp, wait. If it's dry, water thoroughly — enough that water runs out the drainage hole. Then empty the saucer so the roots aren't sitting in water.

Tip: Pots with drainage holes are not optional. Rocks at the bottom of a pot without a hole don't help — they just move the problem deeper.

Light

"Low light" doesn't mean no light — it means no direct sun rays. A room with windows on a cloudy Michigan day is still bright enough for pothos, snake plants, and ZZ plants. "Bright indirect" means near a window but not in the sunbeam. "Direct sun" means on the sill in a south- or west-facing window.

Tip: If a plant is reaching or leaning toward the window, it needs more light. Rotate it a quarter turn every two weeks to keep it growing evenly.

Soil & Pots

Potting soil from the hardware store is fine for most tropical houseplants. For succulents and cacti, mix in perlite at roughly 50/50 to improve drainage. For orchids, use bark. Never put a plant in a pot that's much bigger than its current root ball — too much soil stays wet too long and rots the roots.

Tip: Terracotta pots are more forgiving than plastic because they're breathable and help prevent overwatering. A great choice for beginners or anyone who tends to water too much.

Feeding & Seasons

Feed your plants during the growing season only — roughly April through September here in Michigan. A balanced liquid fertilizer diluted to half strength, once a month, is plenty. In winter, most tropical houseplants are in a rest period. Skip the fertilizer and water less frequently. They're not dying — they're just sleeping.

Tip: Yellow leaves in fall don't always mean something is wrong. If it's happening slowly on lower leaves, it's usually just seasonal adjustment. Sudden widespread yellowing is a different story — usually overwatering.

Quick Reference

Care by plant

The plants we carry most often, and what you need to know about each one.

Golden Pothos (Epipremnum aureum)

Water every 1–2 weeks; let the top 2" dry out. Low to bright indirect light. Mist occasionally in winter when your heat is running and the air gets dry. Fertilize monthly in summer. One of the most forgiving plants we sell.

Low Light OK Not Pet Safe Beginner Friendly

Calathea Orbifolia (Calathea orbifolia)

Water when the top inch dries out — but not bone dry. Prefers filtered or distilled water; tap water can cause brown leaf tips from fluoride. Keep humidity above 50% if possible. A pebble tray with water under the pot makes a noticeable difference in winter. No direct sun.

Indirect Light Pet Safe Humidity Lover

Snake Plant (Dracaena trifasciata)

Water every 2–6 weeks depending on your light level — less in winter, more in summer. Let the soil go completely dry between waterings. Survives low light but grows faster in brighter conditions. Almost impossible to kill by neglect; very easy to kill by overwatering.

Any Light Not Pet Safe Drought Tolerant

Succulents & Cacti

The single biggest mistake: treating them like tropical plants. They need bright, direct or very bright indirect light (a south-facing window). Water thoroughly but infrequently — once every 2–4 weeks in summer, once a month or less in winter. Use cactus mix or add perlite to regular soil. Never mist. Never let them sit in water.

Bright Light Required Pet-Friendly Options Drought Tolerant

Peace Lily (Spathiphyllum)

One of the best plants for telling you what it needs. When the leaves droop slightly, it's thirsty — water deeply and it perks back up within hours. Prefers low to medium indirect light. Blooms occasionally in bright indirect light. Wipe the large leaves with a damp cloth every couple of months to remove dust.

Low Light OK Not Pet Safe Self-Signals
Common Problems

Something going wrong?

Yellow leaves

Usually overwatering — the most common problem. Check your drainage and let the soil dry out more between waterings. If it's just lower leaves yellowing slowly, it may be normal leaf turnover.

Brown leaf tips

Low humidity or fluoride in tap water. Try filtered or distilled water. In winter, run a humidifier or set your plant on a pebble tray with water. Once brown, tips won't green back up — trim them at an angle with clean scissors.

Drooping leaves

Usually either too dry (water it!) or root rot from overwatering (stop watering and check the roots). If the soil is soggy and roots look brown and mushy, it needs repotting into fresh dry mix immediately.

Leggy or reaching

Not enough light. Move it closer to a window or supplement with a grow light. Plants stretch toward light in low conditions — this isn't always deadly but slows growth and weakens the plant over time.

White spots on leaves

Could be mineral deposits from hard water (wipe with a damp cloth), powdery mildew (improve air circulation, reduce humidity around leaves), or spider mites (check the undersides of leaves for fine webbing).

Tiny bugs in the soil

Fungus gnats — annoying but rarely fatal. Let the top 2 inches of soil dry out completely between waterings to interrupt their life cycle. Yellow sticky traps catch the adults. A diluted hydrogen peroxide soil drench kills larvae.
